analysis.one_liner: Exempts farm and forestry stormwater runoff from Clean Water Act pollution permits.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 197 cosponsors but never got a single committee hearing, and it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Clean Water Act so the EPA could not require water pollution permits for stormwater runoff from farms, ranches, orchards, fish farms, or forestry operations. It also would have barred the EPA from pushing states to require those permits on their own, and it would have removed these runoff discharges from the law's core definition of a regulated "point source." In short, it carved agricultural and timber runoff out of the federal water permitting system.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, timber companies and farm operators would have avoided the cost and paperwork of National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System permits for their runoff, and would have gained certainty that no federal or federally-forced state permit requirement could be imposed later.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits the EPA from requiring a Clean Water Act permit for discharges composed entirely of agricultural stormwater, including runoff from cultivated crops, pastures, rangelands, orchards, aquaculture facilities, and forest lands.

It prohibits permits for silviculture operations, defined broadly to include nurseries, reforestation, thinning, prescribed burning, harvest, site preparation, road construction and maintenance, surface drainage, and pest and fire control.
It forbids the EPA from "directly or indirectly" requiring any state to impose such permits, closing off the main route for states to be pushed into regulating this runoff.
It rewrites the Clean Water Act's "point source" definition to exclude agricultural stormwater, irrigation return flows, and forestry stormwater runoff, narrowing the law's basic reach.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would have fallen on people downstream of farms and logged forests. Runoff from fields and forestry work carries sediment, nutrients, and pesticides into rivers, lakes, and drinking water sources, and the bill would have removed the federal permitting backstop for those discharges while tying the EPA's hands on state programs.

drawbacks.text: Agricultural stormwater and forestry runoff are real pollution sources; the exemption would have removed the Clean Water Act permit tool for discharges that can carry sediment, nutrients, and pesticides into public waters.

The silviculture exemption is broad: it covers road construction and maintenance, surface drainage, and harvest operations, not just diffuse field runoff, so even heavy earth-moving and logging-road discharges would go unpermitted.
By barring the EPA from requiring states to regulate this runoff "directly or indirectly," the bill would have eliminated the federal pressure that keeps state programs from backsliding.
Removing these discharges from the "point source" definition narrows the Clean Water Act itself, a structural change that would be hard to undo later.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real argument for the bill: nonpoint runoff is diffuse and hard to regulate through discharge permits, and permitting costs fall hardest on smaller operators. But the bill went further than softening that problem. It swept in logging roads, drainage, and harvest discharges, barred the EPA from influencing state programs at all, and rewrote the Clean Water Act's core definition. The trade was industry regulatory relief bought with weaker protection of the public's water, and the bill never came close to enactment.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and, the next day, to its Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee, where it sat until the 106th Congress ended in January 2001 without any hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jay Dickey introduced the Timber and Agriculture Environmental Fairness Act on February 10, 2000.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure on the day of introduction.
The following day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, and no further action appears in the record.
The bill accumulated 197 cosponsors, including 163 Republicans, 33 Democrats, and 1 Independent, but never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the EPA's existing authority over farm and forestry runoff under the Clean Water Act stayed intact, so the public kept the status quo of federal water pollution oversight. Timber and farm operators did not get the permitting exemption they sought.

for.name: Rep. Jay Dickey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt agricultural stormwater and silviculture operations from Clean Water Act permits.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after receiving the referral; it sat in the Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Support skewed heavily Republican: 163 of 222 House Republicans cosponsored, compared with 33 of 211 Democrats and 1 Independent.

industries.note: The bill would have exempted all silviculture discharges, including logging road construction, drainage, and harvest runoff, from federal pollution permits and blocked states from being made to require them. The industry's gain was the public's loss of a clean-water backstop.
Agricultural stormwater discharges would have been permanently freed from permit requirements, sparing operators compliance costs while runoff entered public waters unpermitted.
Stormwater runoff from aquaculture facilities was expressly included in the agricultural stormwater exemption.
